title: Adaptive prefetch and fusion field notes
content:
Context:
These are field notes from a short spike exploring adaptive prefetch heuristics and the runtime cost of kernel fusion for attention paths. Goal: reduce 95th/99th tail without regressing average throughput for mixed-length workloads (small chat turns + occasional >2k seqs). Work happened on a small fleet of A10/RTX8000 test nodes; traces collected with tracebench and custom hoplog hooks.

Summary / TL;DR: 
- FlashAttention (FA) gives best steady-state throughput on long sequences when kernels stay warm and memory is contiguous.
- Paged attention (PA) helps memory-constrained workloads by limiting activation residency, but introduces latency jitter from page-in costs and kernel switch overhead.
- Fused-ops kernel (FO) reduces kernel launch overheads at small batch sizes, but increases register pressure causing occasional long-tail stalls on >1024 sequence lengths.
- Adaptive prefetch (AP) that biases KV cache retention for recent prefixes + opportunistic prefetch on expected continuation points (based on prompt length distribution) reduced 95th latency by ~18% in our mixed workload trace without reducing throughput.

Hypotheses we tested: 
1) Prefetching entire KV on short-turns wastes bandwidth; partial prefix prefetch based on token probability distribution can save memory bandwidth.
2) Kernel fusion avoids CPU/GPU synchronization for small-batch chat queries, but fused kernels can become memory-bound earlier, losing benefits for long seqs.
3) Switching from FA to PA mid-request (hybrid) is high-overhead due to kernel-state translation (KV layout conversion) unless we maintain an intermediate fast-convert format.

Experiment matrix (short):
- Variables: kernel_type in {FlashAttention, PagedAttention, FusedOps}, prefetch_strategy in {none, full_kv, adaptive_partial}, batch_shapes = [single_small(1x64), burst_small(8x64), mixed_streams(uniform 1-2048)]
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) for token step, GPU util, SM occupancy, memory copy time, kernel-launch time, KV-conversion time (if any), end-to-end tokens/sec.

Representative commands used: 
- tracebench run --config spike-mixed-2025.json --collect=hoplog,devtools
- nvprof equivalent traces collected with NSYS (limited sampling due to perf impact)
- instrumented: serving-runtime/component/kv_cache metrics (hit_rate, evictions, prefetch_ops)

Key raw observations (spot samples):
- Mixed_streams + FA + no prefetch:
  p50 token latency: 12ms, p95: 78ms, p99: 210ms, tokens/sec: 4.2k
  Notes: large p99 from cold-activation page-ins on >1024 seqs.
- Mixed_streams + FA + adaptive_partial_prefetch:
  p50: 11.6ms, p95: 64ms, p99: 162ms, tokens/sec: 4.15k
  Notes: smaller gains on p50, larger tail improvement due to avoiding full KV copy on many short queries.
- Mixed_streams + PagedAttention + adaptive_partial_prefetch:
  p50: 13ms, p95: 69ms, p99: 170ms, tokens/sec: 3.9k
  Notes: throughput drop but tail similar to FA+adaptive. Page-in spikes still present for >2k sequences.
- Mixed_streams + FusedOps + no prefetch (small-batch burst workload):
  p50: 9.8ms, p95: 46ms, p99: 112ms, tokens/sec: 4.6k
  Notes: excellent small-batch latency; however observed occasional 400-800ms stalls correlated with register/spill cycles in sm_8x kernels for >1k seqs.

Profiling notes: 
- Kernel-launch time contribution is significant for single-token small-batch queries. FusedOp reduces the number of kernel launches by ~40% in our microbench harness.
- Memory copies (device<->device and device<->host) were 2x higher in full-KV prefetch; adaptive_partial kept copies closer to working set.
- KV-layout conversion (FA <-> PA) cost ranges 1.2ms - 18ms depending on sequence length and whether we do a streaming converter vs naive copy. This explains why hybrid switching mid-request is expensive.
- Page-in cost spikes: when paged-attention triggers page fault paths, observed up to 120ms stall for single request (rare but catastrophic for SLAs).

Adaptive prefetch heuristic we prototyped: 
- Maintain per-route rolling histogram of observed continuation lengths and LRU rank of keys.
- If predicted remaining tokens <= 64, prefetch only recent 2-4 KV blocks (partial). If predicted > 512, prefetch full KV incrementally (in background) and pin first pages.
- Backoff policy: if GPU mem pressure > threshold or prefetch queue backlog grows, reduce prefetch aggressiveness for low-priority requests.
- Implementation notes: prefetch implemented as async CUDA memcpy streams with priority (low for background). Ensured we cancel outstanding prefetches on early termination to avoid wasted bandwidth.

Tradeoffs / open questions: 
- How to pick the predictor? We used an exponential moving average on route-level continuation lengths and also fed small LLM that predicted continuation length from prompt context; latter is promising but adds model-in-loop cost.
- Is the complexity worth it? For PLG routes with many tiny chat steps, AP reduces SLO breaches. For compute-heavy long-form routes, AP adds no value and adds complexity. Maybe per-customer or per-route config.
- Conversion format: should we introduce a canonical KV representation that both FA and PA can reference to reduce switch costs? That would require a short-lived jitted converter or memory layout that both kernels accept.
- FusedOps stability: can we reduce spill by splitting fused kernels by sequence length bands or adding dynamic shared-memory tuning?

Actions and TODOs: 
- (A) Add lightweight route-level continuation predictor metrics to Console for a week-long A/B. Owner: Arjun. Timeline: 2 weeks.
- (B) Prototype intermediate KV layout that supports zero-copy view for FA/PA kernel variants. Owner: Maya. Timeline: 3 sprints.
- (C) Implement prefetch backpressure telemetry (queue sizes, mem pressure). Owner: Lena. Timeline: 1 sprint.
- (D) Run long-duration soak with mixed_streams workload for 72 hours with AP on/off to quantify SLO impact. Owner: Diego. Timeline: next week.

Notes for future benchmarks: 
- Add a 'conversion time' column to bench harness and log format to capture FA<->PA translation cost explicitly.
- Introduce synthetic spike workload that simulates burst of long context generation to measure page-in event frequency.
- For fused ops, collect register pressure counters and L2 miss counters to pinpoint spill triggers.

Appendix: quick checklist of reproducibility steps
- Checkout: git@github.com:redwood-inference/serving-runtime.git spike/adaptive-prefetch
- Build: bazel build //runtime:bench_driver --config=dev-nsight
- Run harness: ./bazel-bin/runtime/bench_driver --scenario mixed_streams --profile hoplog --out /tmp/bench/mixed_ap
- Collect traces: nsys profile --output /tmp/nsys/mixed_ap --trace=cuda,osrt -- ./bazel-bin/runtime/bench_driver --scenario mixed_streams

Random notes / gotchas observed during spike: 
- Some GPUs (older Ampere variants) show better behavior under PA because their memory subsystem tolerates scattered accesses better. Not uniform across fleet.
- Prefetch cancellation races: need to deconflict with eviction path; previously saw double-free-like metrics when prefetch and eviction collided.
- Small-batch fused kernels are great for PLG but complicate rollouts because A/B testing kernel variants causes noisy client-side performance signals unless routed properly.

Questions for review: 
- Prioritize (B) canonical KV layout vs (A) predictor telemetry? Which yields bigger ops win faster?
- Acceptable operational complexity for per-route prefetch? Should default be off for enterprise until stable?

End of notes.
